name: Alhambra
history: Built mostly by the Nasrid dynasty in the 13th and 14th centuries on the Sabika hill above Granada, the Alhambra ('the red one', after the colour of its walls) was a fortress, palace and small city in one. Its Court of the Lions and Hall of the Ambassadors are masterpieces of Islamic art, covered in carved stucco, honeycomb muqarnas vaults and inscribed poetry. When Granada fell to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492, the Catholic Monarchs moved in, and Charles V later added a Renaissance palace. Washington Irving's Tales of the Alhambra (1832) revived its fame across Europe.

name: Amundsen-Scott Research Station
history: Named for Roald Amundsen and Robert Falcon Scott, whose rival expeditions reached the South Pole in December 1911 and January 1912, the station was first built by the US Navy in 1956–57 for the International Geophysical Year. It has been continuously occupied ever since, rebuilt under a geodesic dome in 1975 and replaced by today's elevated station in 2008. The cold, dry and stable air over the polar plateau makes it one of the best places on Earth for astronomy, and it hosts the South Pole Telescope and the IceCube neutrino observatory buried in the ice below.

name: Angkor Wat
history: Built in the early 12th century by the Khmer king Suryavarman II as a temple to Vishnu and probably his own funerary monument, Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world. Its five lotus-bud towers represent Mount Meru, home of the gods, and its vast moat stands for the cosmic ocean. By the end of the century it was gradually becoming a Buddhist temple, and unlike most of Angkor it was never fully abandoned. Its silhouette appears on Cambodia's national flag.

name: Apadana
history: The Apadana was the great audience hall of the Achaemenid Persian kings at Persepolis, begun under Darius the Great around 515 BCE and completed by his son Xerxes. A forest of towering stone columns, crowned with carved bulls and lions, held up a roof of cedar beams. Its staircases are lined with reliefs of delegations from across the empire, from Lydians and Ethiopians to Indians and Scythians, bringing gifts to the King of Kings. Alexander the Great burned Persepolis in 330 BCE, but thirteen of its columns still stand.

name: Big Ben
history: Big Ben is properly the nickname of the 13.7-tonne Great Bell inside the clock tower of the Palace of Westminster, though the name is now used for the whole tower, officially renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012. The tower was designed by Augustus Pugin as part of Charles Barry's rebuilding of Parliament after the great fire of 1834, and its clock began keeping time in 1859. Famous for its reliability, the clock is still fine-tuned by adding or removing old penny coins on its pendulum.

name: Biosphère
history: The Biosphère began life as the United States pavilion at Expo 67 in Montreal: a 76-metre geodesic dome designed by the visionary engineer Buckminster Fuller. Its transparent acrylic skin burned away in a fire in 1976, leaving only the steel lattice standing. Since 1995 it has housed a museum devoted to the environment, climate and water, which is why Civilization VI uses it as a clean-energy wonder.

name: Bolshoi Theatre
history: The Bolshoi ('Grand') Theatre traces its origins to 1776, when Catherine the Great licensed Prince Pyotr Urusov to stage performances in Moscow. Its neoclassical building, with an eight-column portico topped by Apollo's bronze chariot, opened in 1825 and was rebuilt by Alberto Cavos after a fire in 1853. Its ballet company is one of the oldest and most celebrated in the world and gave the first performance of Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake in 1877. A six-year restoration completed in 2011 brought back its famous acoustics.

name: Broadway
history: Broadway is both one of the oldest streets in Manhattan, following the line of an old Native American trail, and shorthand for the large professional theatres clustered around Times Square. Theatres moved uptown to the area around the turn of the 20th century, and its glowing marquees earned the street the nickname 'the Great White Way'. From Show Boat and Oklahoma! to West Side Story and Hamilton, it became the heart of American musical theatre and one of the country's great cultural exports.

name: Casa de Contratación
history: Established by the Catholic Monarchs in Seville in 1503, the House of Trade controlled all Spanish shipping and commerce with the Americas. It licensed ships, collected the crown's share of New World silver and gold, trained navigators and kept the Padrón Real, a secret master map of every Spanish discovery. Amerigo Vespucci became its first chief pilot in 1508. As the river to Seville silted up it moved to Cádiz in 1717, and it was abolished in 1790.

name: Chichen Itza
history: Chichén Itzá was one of the largest Maya cities, flourishing on the Yucatán Peninsula from roughly 600 to 1200 CE. Its stepped pyramid, El Castillo or the Temple of Kukulcán, is a calendar in stone: its four stairways of 91 steps plus the top platform total 365. At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the afternoon sun casts a serpent of light that seems to slither down the northern stairway. The city also boasts the largest ball court in ancient Mesoamerica and the Sacred Cenote, where offerings, and people, were sacrificed to the rain god.

name: Colosseum
history: Begun by Emperor Vespasian around 70 CE and opened by his son Titus in 80 CE with 100 days of games, the Flavian Amphitheatre is the largest amphitheatre ever built, holding an estimated 50,000 or more spectators. For over four centuries it staged gladiator fights, wild animal hunts, executions and re-enactments of famous battles, with a maze of tunnels and lifts beneath the arena floor. Earthquakes and centuries of stone robbing took their toll, but it remains the enduring symbol of Imperial Rome.

name: Colossus
history: The Colossus of Rhodes was a bronze statue of the sun god Helios, raised by the Rhodians around 280 BCE to celebrate surviving a year-long siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes, partly paid for by selling the siege equipment he left behind. About 33 metres tall, roughly the height of the Statue of Liberty from heel to head, it was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It stood for only about 54 years before an earthquake snapped it at the knees in 226 BCE. Despite the famous image, it almost certainly did not straddle the harbour.

name: Cristo Redentor
history: The 30-metre Art Deco statue of Christ with outstretched arms stands on the 700-metre peak of Corcovado above Rio de Janeiro. Designed by French sculptor Paul Landowski, engineered by Brazilian Heitor da Silva Costa, with the face sculpted by Romanian artist Gheorghe Leonida, it was built of reinforced concrete covered in a mosaic of soapstone tiles between 1922 and 1931. Struck by lightning several times a year, it has become the symbol of Rio and of Brazil, and was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.

name: Eiffel Tower
history: Gustave Eiffel's company built the tower as the entrance arch to the 1889 World's Fair, which marked the centenary of the French Revolution. Many Parisian artists and writers denounced it as a monstrosity, and it was meant to stand for only 20 years, but it proved valuable as a radio antenna and was saved. At 300 metres it was the tallest man-made structure in the world until 1930, and it is now one of the most visited paid monuments on Earth.

name: Estádio do Maracanã
history: Built for the 1950 FIFA World Cup, the Maracanã was then the largest stadium in the world; an estimated 200,000 people watched Uruguay stun Brazil 2–1 in the deciding match, a defeat Brazilians still call the Maracanazo. Pelé scored his 1,000th goal here in 1969. Rebuilt and modernised several times, it hosted the 2014 World Cup final and the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2016 Summer Olympics.

name: Etemenanki
history: Etemenanki, Sumerian for 'temple of the foundation of heaven and earth', was the great ziggurat of Marduk at the heart of Babylon. Rebuilt to its final, roughly 90-metre form by Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II in the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, it is widely thought to have inspired the biblical story of the Tower of Babel. Alexander the Great had it cleared away intending to rebuild it, but died before work began. Today only the outline of its foundations survives, in a marshy pit.

name: Forbidden City
history: Built between 1406 and 1420 under the Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty, the Forbidden City was home to 24 emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties for nearly 500 years. Ordinary people could not enter without the emperor's permission, hence the name. Its roughly 980 surviving buildings, with yellow-glazed roofs reserved for the emperor, cover 72 hectares, making it the largest preserved palace complex in the world. After the last emperor, Puyi, was expelled, it became the Palace Museum in 1925.

name: Golden Gate Bridge
history: Spanning the strait that links San Francisco Bay to the Pacific Ocean, the Golden Gate Bridge opened in 1937 after four years of work through fog, fierce currents and high winds. Its 1,280-metre main span was the longest in the world until 1964. Chief engineer Joseph Strauss led the project, while architect Irving Morrow gave it its Art Deco towers and its famous 'International Orange' paint, chosen to stand out in the fog and blend with the hills.

name: Great Bath
history: The Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro, built around 2500 BCE by the Indus Valley Civilisation, is one of the earliest public water tanks in the ancient world. About 12 by 7 metres and 2.4 metres deep, it was made watertight with tightly fitted bricks, gypsum mortar and a layer of bitumen, and was fed by a nearby well. Its exact purpose is unknown, since the Indus script has never been deciphered, but it is generally thought to have been used for ritual bathing and purification.

name: Great Library
history: Founded in the early 3rd century BCE under the first Ptolemies, the Library of Alexandria set out to collect every book in the known world; ships docking in the harbour reportedly had their scrolls seized and copied. Scholars such as Eratosthenes, who measured the circumference of the Earth, and the poet Callimachus worked there. Its destruction was not a single great fire but a long decline, through Caesar's fire of 48 BCE, purges of scholars and the decline of Roman Alexandria. Its exact site is unknown; the modern Bibliotheca Alexandrina (marked here) opened in its honour in 2002.

name: Great Lighthouse
history: Completed around 280 BCE on the island of Pharos, the Lighthouse of Alexandria guided ships into Egypt's busiest port with a fire, and possibly a great mirror, at its summit. Over 100 metres tall, it was among the tallest man-made structures in the world for centuries and one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Damaged by a series of earthquakes, it was in ruins by the 14th century, and in 1480 the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built a fortress on its foundations. 'Pharos' became the word for lighthouse in Greek, French, Italian and Spanish.

name: Great Zimbabwe
history: Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a Shona kingdom that flourished from the 11th to the 15th century, growing rich on cattle and on the gold and ivory trade that ran through Swahili ports to Arabia, India and China. Its Great Enclosure is the largest ancient stone structure south of the Sahara, with walls up to 11 metres high built from granite blocks fitted together without mortar. Colonial-era writers falsely credited it to foreign builders; archaeology proved its African origins, and the newly independent country took its name, meaning 'houses of stone', in 1980.

name: Hagia Sophia
history: Built in under six years and completed in 537 CE for the Byzantine emperor Justinian I, Hagia Sophia ('Holy Wisdom') has a vast dome that seems to float on a ring of windows, and it was the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years. Its architects, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, used pendentives to set a round dome over a square hall on an unprecedented scale. After the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 it became a mosque, then a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

name: Hanging Gardens
history: Greek and Roman writers described terraced gardens of trees and flowers rising like a green mountain in Babylon, said to have been built by Nebuchadnezzar II around 600 BCE for his homesick wife Amytis, who missed the hills of Media. They are the only one of the Seven Wonders whose site has never been found, and no surviving Babylonian text mentions them. Some historians believe they were purely legendary; others, notably Stephanie Dalley, argue they were really the gardens of the Assyrian king Sennacherib at Nineveh, far to the north.

name: Hermitage
history: Catherine the Great founded the Hermitage in 1764 when she bought a collection of over 200 paintings, which she displayed in a private 'hermitage' wing of the Winter Palace. Opened to the public in 1852, the museum now holds more than three million objects, from Scythian gold to works by Leonardo, Rembrandt and Matisse. It spans six historic buildings along the Neva, including the green-and-white Baroque Winter Palace, the former residence of the Russian tsars, which was stormed during the October Revolution of 1917.

name: Huey Teocalli
history: Huey Teocalli ('great house of the gods') was the Templo Mayor, the twin-shrined pyramid at the sacred heart of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital built on an island in Lake Texcoco. Its two temples honoured Huitzilopochtli, god of war and the sun, and Tlaloc, god of rain. Enlarged at least seven times between about 1325 and 1521, it was torn down by the Spanish after the conquest, and Mexico City rose over its ruins. It was rediscovered in 1978, when electrical workers struck a huge carved stone of the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui.

name: Jebel Barkal
history: Jebel Barkal is a flat-topped sandstone mountain beside the Nile in Sudan, whose cliff face has a pinnacle that resembles a rearing cobra wearing a royal crown. The Egyptians, who conquered Nubia around 1450 BCE, believed it was a home of the god Amun and built a great temple at its foot. The Kushite kings of Napata later made it their holiest site, and from here King Piye marched north to conquer Egypt around 727 BCE, founding the 25th Dynasty of pharaohs. Pyramids, temples and palaces still surround the mountain.

name: Kilwa Kisiwani
history: On a small island off the coast of Tanzania, Kilwa Kisiwani grew into the most powerful of the Swahili city-states, controlling the gold trade from the Zimbabwe plateau through the port of Sofala. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta, visiting in 1331, called it one of the most beautiful and well-built cities in the world. Its coral-stone Great Mosque and the enormous palace of Husuni Kubwa survive as ruins. The Portuguese sacked the city in 1505, and it never regained its former wealth.

name: Kotoku-in
history: Kōtoku-in is a Pure Land Buddhist temple in Kamakura, famous for its Great Buddha: a bronze statue of Amida Buddha more than 13 metres tall including its base, cast from around 1252. It originally sat inside a great wooden hall, but the building was destroyed by storms and finally washed away by a tsunami in 1498, and the Buddha has sat in the open air ever since. The statue is hollow, and visitors can step inside it.

name: Machu Picchu
history: Built around 1450 as a royal estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti, Machu Picchu sits on a mountain ridge about 2,430 metres above sea level in the Peruvian Andes. Its dry-stone walls are cut so precisely that a knife blade cannot fit between some blocks, and the site was engineered with terraces and drainage to survive heavy rains and earthquakes. Abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest, it was never found by the conquistadors. Hiram Bingham brought it to international attention in 1911.

name: Mahabodhi Temple
history: The Mahabodhi Temple marks the place in Bodh Gaya where Siddhartha Gautama is said to have attained enlightenment under a Bodhi tree, making it the holiest site in Buddhism. The emperor Ashoka built the first shrine here in the 3rd century BCE; the present 55-metre temple dates largely from the 5th and 6th centuries CE and is one of the oldest brick temples surviving in India. A descendant of the original Bodhi tree still grows beside it, and pilgrims come from across the Buddhist world.

name: Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
history: The Mausoleum was the tomb of Mausolus, a ruler of Caria under the Persian Empire, built around 350 BCE by his wife and sister Artemisia II. Designed by Greek architects and decorated by four of the most famous sculptors of the age, it stood around 45 metres tall and was so admired that his name became the word for any grand tomb. Earthquakes had toppled it by the 15th century, and the Knights of St John reused its stones to build Bodrum Castle. Some of its sculptures survive in the British Museum.

name: Meenakshi Temple
history: The Meenakshi Amman Temple in Madurai is dedicated to the goddess Meenakshi, a form of Parvati, and her consort Sundareswarar, a form of Shiva. Madurai has been a temple city for more than two thousand years, but the present complex was largely built by the Nayak rulers in the 16th and 17th centuries after earlier shrines were damaged in 14th-century raids. Its 14 gopurams (gateway towers), the tallest about 52 metres high, are covered in thousands of brightly painted figures of gods, animals and demons.

name: Mont St. Michel
history: According to legend, the archangel Michael appeared in 708 to Aubert, Bishop of Avranches, and commanded him to build a church on this rocky tidal island off the Normandy coast. A Benedictine abbey founded in 966 grew over the centuries into a Gothic marvel stacked up the rock. Protected by some of the strongest tides in Europe, the fortified mount was never captured by the English during the Hundred Years' War. It later served as a prison before becoming one of the most visited sites in France.

name: Oracle
when: Active c. 8th century BCE – 4th century CE
history: From around the 8th century BCE, Greeks travelled to Delphi on the slopes of Mount Parnassus to consult the Pythia, the priestess of Apollo, whose prophecies were believed to come from the god himself. Kings and city-states sought her advice before wars and before founding colonies, and the Greeks considered Delphi the omphalos, the navel of the world. The sanctuary also hosted the Pythian Games. The oracle declined under Roman rule and fell silent by the end of the 4th century CE, as the Christian empire suppressed pagan sanctuaries.

name: Országház
history: The Hungarian Parliament Building on the bank of the Danube was designed by Imre Steindl in a Gothic Revival style inspired by London's Palace of Westminster. Built between 1885 and 1904, it was inaugurated in 1896 for the thousandth anniversary of the Magyar settlement of the Carpathian Basin, and its central dome is 96 metres tall in a nod to the year 896. With 691 rooms it is the largest building in Hungary. Steindl went blind before it was finished and died weeks before its completion.

name: Oxford University
history: Teaching existed at Oxford by 1096, making it the oldest university in the English-speaking world, and it grew rapidly after Henry II barred English students from the University of Paris in 1167. It is a federation of more than thirty self-governing colleges, from medieval Merton and Balliol to Christ Church. Its alumni include dozens of British prime ministers, scientists from Robert Hooke to Stephen Hawking, and writers such as J. R. R. Tolkien and C. S. Lewis. Its Bodleian Library, opened in 1602, is one of the oldest in Europe.

name: Panama Canal
history: The 82-kilometre Panama Canal cuts across the Isthmus of Panama, sparing ships the long and dangerous voyage around Cape Horn. A French attempt led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, builder of the Suez Canal, collapsed in the 1880s amid bankruptcy and around 22,000 deaths, mostly from yellow fever and malaria. The United States took over in 1904 and, after bringing the mosquito-borne diseases under control, opened the canal in 1914, using locks to lift ships 26 metres to the artificial Gatún Lake. Panama took full control in 1999, and larger locks opened in 2016.

name: Petra
when: Nabataean capital from c. 4th century BCE
history: Petra was the rose-red capital of the Nabataeans, Arab traders who grew rich controlling the incense and spice caravan routes. They carved temples and tombs straight into the sandstone cliffs and engineered dams, channels and cisterns to store the scarce desert rain. Its most famous façade, Al-Khazneh (the Treasury), is reached through the Siq, a narrow gorge more than a kilometre long. Annexed by Rome in 106 CE, the city faded as trade routes shifted and after an earthquake in 363, and was rediscovered for Europe by Johann Ludwig Burckhardt in 1812.

name: Potala Palace
history: Rising thirteen storeys above Lhasa on the Red Hill, the Potala Palace was begun in 1645 by the 5th Dalai Lama on the site of a 7th-century palace of King Songtsen Gampo. It served as the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas and the seat of Tibetan government until the 14th Dalai Lama fled to India in 1959. Its White Palace held living quarters and offices, while the Red Palace contains chapels, thousands of statues and the gilded burial stupas of past Dalai Lamas.

name: Pyramids
history: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BCE as the tomb of the pharaoh Khufu, followed by the pyramids of his successors Khafre and Menkaure. Some 2.3 million stone blocks went into the Great Pyramid, which at about 146 metres remained the tallest man-made structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years. Contrary to popular myth, it was built not by slaves but by organised, paid crews of workers, whose village has been excavated nearby. It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one still standing.

name: Ruhr Valley
history: The Ruhr in western Germany sits on one of Europe's richest coal fields, and in the 19th century it became the industrial heart of the German Empire, crowded with coal mines, steelworks and the Krupp industrial empire in Essen. Its output powered Germany through two world wars, and France and Belgium occupied it in 1923 when Germany fell behind on reparations. After the long decline of coal and steel, the last hard-coal mine closed in 2018, and sites such as the Zollverein Coal Mine in Essen (marked here) became museums, parks and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: St. Basil's Cathedral
history: Ivan the Terrible commissioned the Cathedral of the Intercession on Red Square in 1555 to celebrate his conquest of the Khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan. Completed in 1561, it is a cluster of chapels arranged around a central tower, each crowned by its own distinctive onion dome; the vivid colours were added in later centuries. A legend claims Ivan had the architects blinded so they could never build anything as beautiful again, a tale historians doubt. Its popular name honours St. Basil the Holy Fool, buried in a chapel added in 1588.

name: Statue of Liberty
history: Liberty Enlightening the World was a gift from the people of France to the United States, designed by sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi with an internal iron framework engineered by Gustave Eiffel. Dedicated in 1886 in New York Harbor, its copper skin, only a few millimetres thick, has weathered to its famous green patina. Holding a torch aloft and a tablet inscribed with the date of the Declaration of Independence, it became a symbol of welcome for millions of immigrants arriving at nearby Ellis Island.

name: Statue of Zeus
history: Created by the Athenian sculptor Phidias around 435 BCE, the Statue of Zeus sat enthroned in the god's temple at Olympia, home of the ancient Olympic Games. About 12 metres tall, it was built of ivory and gold panels over a wooden frame, and ancient writers joked that if Zeus stood up he would lift the roof off the temple. Phidias's workshop has been excavated nearby, complete with a cup inscribed 'I belong to Phidias'. The statue was lost in the 5th century CE, probably in a fire after being carried off to Constantinople.

name: Stonehenge
history: Built in stages from about 3000 to 1500 BCE on Salisbury Plain, Stonehenge combines huge sarsen stones weighing up to 25 tonnes with smaller 'bluestones' hauled more than 200 kilometres from the Preseli Hills of Wales. Its main axis aligns with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset, suggesting a ceremonial and perhaps calendrical purpose, and it was also used as a cemetery from its earliest days. How Neolithic people moved and raised the stones without metal tools or the wheel remains one of archaeology's great questions.

name: Sydney Opera House
history: Danish architect Jørn Utzon won an international design competition in 1957 with his vision of sail-like shells on Bennelong Point in Sydney Harbour. Construction, begun in 1959, was plagued by engineering problems and soaring costs; the breakthrough came when the shells were redesigned as sections of a single sphere. Utzon resigned in 1966 amid disputes with the government and never returned to see it finished. Opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1973, it was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007, a year before Utzon's death.

name: Taj Mahal
history: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan began the Taj Mahal in 1632 as a mausoleum for his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died giving birth to their fourteenth child. Some 20,000 artisans worked on the white marble tomb, inlaid with semi-precious stones and Quranic calligraphy, and on its gardens, mosque and guest house, finished around 1653. Shah Jahan was later deposed by his son Aurangzeb and confined in Agra Fort, where tradition says he spent his final years gazing at the Taj across the Yamuna. He is buried beside Mumtaz.

name: Temple of Artemis
history: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, on the Aegean coast of present-day Turkey, was rebuilt several times. Its most famous version, funded in part by the fabulously rich Lydian king Croesus around 550 BCE, was one of the first great marble temples of the Greek world. In 356 BCE a man named Herostratus burned it down purely to make himself famous; legend says it happened the same night Alexander the Great was born. Rebuilt even larger, it was later damaged by raiders and abandoned. Today a single re-erected column marks the site.

name: Terracotta Army
history: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an found fragments of what turned out to be an estimated 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers, with horses and chariots, buried to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China, who died in 210 BCE. Every soldier has individual features and was originally brightly painted. The emperor's burial mound itself, said by the historian Sima Qian to contain rivers of flowing mercury, has still not been opened.

name: Torre de Belém
history: Built between 1514 and 1519 on the Tagus River in Lisbon, the Tower of Belém was a fortress guarding the harbour and a ceremonial gateway for Portugal's Age of Discovery, near where Vasco da Gama set out for India in 1497. Its lavish Manueline style blends late Gothic stonework with maritime motifs such as twisted ropes and armillary spheres, and even a carved rhinoceros, thought to depict the rhino that arrived in Lisbon in 1515 and was famously drawn by Albrecht Dürer.

name: University of Sankore
history: The Sankore Mosque in Timbuktu was the heart of a great Islamic centre of learning that flourished under the Mali and Songhai empires in the 14th to 16th centuries. Rather than a single campus, it was a network of independent scholars teaching law, theology, astronomy, mathematics and medicine to students from across West Africa and beyond. Timbuktu's families collected hundreds of thousands of manuscripts over the centuries, and many were smuggled to safety when militants occupied the city in 2012.

name: Venetian Arsenal
history: Founded around 1104, the Arsenale was the state shipyard and armoury of the Republic of Venice, and at its height it employed thousands of skilled workers. Using standardised parts and a production line along its canals, it could reportedly assemble a war galley in a single day, centuries before the industrial assembly line. Dante described its vats of boiling pitch in the Inferno. Its fleets secured Venice's maritime empire for centuries, and parts of it now host the Venice Biennale.
